claim: The shapes of mammalian whiskers are diverse.

claim: Human hair is approximately cylindrical.

claim: Whiskers of harbor seals have elliptical cross-sections with an undulated structure.
source: Whiskers of harbor seals have elliptical cross-sections with an undulated structure (Hanke et al., 2010).

claim: Differences in whisker shapes across different species likely reflect differences in how animals use their whiskers.

source: For example, the undulating microstructure of harbor seal whiskers suppresses vibrations triggered by vortices and enhances the seal's ability to analyze water movements (Hanke et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hanke et al., 2010.

claim: Rodents sense their surroundings by moving their whiskers over objects with large amplitudes (up to 50° peak–peak) in a rhythmic motion.
source: Rodents sense their surroundings by moving their whiskers over objects with large amplitudes (up to 50° peak–peak) in a rhythmic motion (Knutsen et al., 2006; O'Connor et al., 2010a; O'Connor et al., 2013; Voigts et al., 2008).

claim: Rodents can localize and recognize objects in three dimensions.

claim: Rodents can discriminate subtle differences in surface textures.
source: and also discriminate subtle differences in surface textures (Carvell and Simons, 1990; Wolfe et al., 2008) (reviewed in Diamond, 2010).

claim: Rodent tactile behaviors are based on collisions between whiskers and objects, which cause time-varying forces at the whisker base and excitation of sensory neurons in the follicles.

claim: Whisker mechanics couples the tactile world to forces at the whisker base.
source: Whisker mechanics thus couples the tactile world to forces at the whisker base (Solomon and Hartmann, 2006; Birdwell et al., 2007; Bagdasarian et al., 2013; Pammer et al., 2013).

claim: Rodent whiskers are thin, approximately linear and homogenous elastic cones.
source: Rodent whiskers are thin, approximately linear and homogenous elastic cones (Solomon and Hartmann, 2006; Birdwell et al., 2007; Williams and Kramer, 2010; Pammer et al., 2013).

claim: As a result of the linear taper, whisker bending stiffness decreases with distance from the face over five orders of magnitude.
source: As a result of the linear taper, whisker bending stiffness decreases with distance from the face over five orders of magnitude.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the conical geometry and material properties of whiskers.

claim: Behavioral measurements have shown that mice use distance-dependent whisker mechanics as a ruler to estimate object location along the length of the whisker.
source: Behavioral measurements have shown that mice use distance-dependent whisker mechanics as a ruler to estimate object location along the length of the whisker (Pammer et al., 2013).

claim: Conical whiskers sweep across textures with informative micromotions, whereas cylindrical whiskers get stuck.
source: Conical whiskers sweep across textures with informative micromotions, whereas cylindrical whiskers get stuck.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: The steep increase in flexibility from base to tip of conical whiskers allow rodents to maneuver their sensors past objects with relative ease.
source: The steep increase in flexibility from base to tip of conical whiskers allow rodents to maneuver their sensors past objects with relative ease.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and theoretical modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: Conical whisker shape is critical for tactile exploration in confined spaces.
source: Conical whisker shape is thus critical for tactile exploration in confined spaces.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental and theoretical results.

claim: When pushed into objects, conical whiskers suddenly slip at a critical angle.
source: When pushed into objects, conical whiskers suddenly slip at a critical angle.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 5 and theoretical modeling in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Cylindrical whiskers do not slip for biologically plausible movements.
source: In contrast, cylindrical whiskers do not slip for biologically plausible movements.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4 and theoretical modeling in Figure 3.

claim: Conical whiskers sweep across objects and textures in characteristic sequences of brief sticks and slips, which provide information about the tactile world.
source: Conical whiskers sweep across objects and textures in characteristic sequences of brief sticks and slips, which provide information about the tactile world.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: Cylindrical whiskers stick and remain stuck, even when sweeping across fine textures.
source: In contrast, cylindrical whiskers stick and remain stuck, even when sweeping across fine textures.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: The conical whisker structure is adaptive for sensor mobility in constrained environments.
source: Thus the conical whisker structure is adaptive for sensor mobility in constrained environments and in feature extraction during active haptic exploration of objects and surfaces.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental and theoretical results.

claim: The conical whisker structure is adaptive for feature extraction during active haptic exploration of objects and surfaces.
source: Thus the conical whisker structure is adaptive for sensor mobility in constrained environments and in feature extraction during active haptic exploration of objects and surfaces.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental and theoretical results.

claim: The boundary-value problem for whisker shape generally has two solutions, one stable and the other unstable.
source: The boundary-value problem for whisker shape generally has two solutions, one stable and the other unstable (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by theoretical modeling shown in Figure 2A.

claim: During object contact, the whisker shape matches the stable solution since small perturbations from it will decay back to the stable solution.
source: During object contact, the whisker shape matches the stable solution since small perturbations from it will decay back to the stable solution (Strogatz, 1994).
evidence: The claim is based on established dynamical systems theory, cited to Strogatz, 1994.

claim: As the whisker pushes further into the object it becomes increasingly deflected.
source: As the whisker pushes further into the object it becomes increasingly deflected (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by theoretical modeling shown in Figure 2B.

claim: As the whisker pushes into the object, the whisker slides along the object and the arclength from the whisker base to the point of contact, sobj, increases until the whisker detaches from the object.
source: At the same time the whisker slides along the object and the arclength from the whisker base to the point of contact, sobj, increases until the whisker detaches from the object.
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical modeling results.

claim: Under some conditions detachment occurs suddenly before the end of the whisker has reached the object, sobj < LW; this type of detachment is referred to as 'slip-off'.
source: First, under some conditions detachment occurs suddenly before the end of the whisker has reached the object, sobj < LW; we refer to this type of detachment as 'slip-off' (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by theoretical modeling shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Detachment occurs when the tip reaches the end of the object, sobj = LW; this type of detachment is referred to as 'pull-off'.
source: Second, detachment has to occur when the tip reaches the end of the object, sobj = LW; we refer to this type of detachment as 'pull-off' (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by theoretical modeling shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: For conical whiskers, at a critical θp, the two solutions coalesce and disappear at a saddle-node bifurcation.
source: At a critical θp, the two solutions (solid lines, dashed lines) coalesce and disappear at a saddle-node bifurcation (SNB) (Strogatz, 1994) (Figure 3B–D, solid circles).
evidence: The claim is supported by theoretical modeling shown in Figure 3B-D and cited to Strogatz, 1994.

claim: No solution exists above the critical θp value for conical whiskers, which also corresponds to a critical sobj < LW.
source: No solution exists above this critical θp value, which also corresponds to a critical sobj < LW.
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical modeling results.

claim: The saddle-node bifurcation corresponds to slip-off.
source: The saddle-node bifurcation corresponds to slip-off.
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical modeling and interpretation.

claim: In the CF configuration, sobj first decreases as |θp| increases from 0, because touch forces straighten the whisker.
source: In the CF configuration, sobj first decreases as |θp| increases from 0, because touch forces straighten the whisker (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by theoretical modeling shown in Figure 3D.

claim: With further increases in θp in the CF configuration, the whisker bends in the other direction and sobj increases.
source: With further increases in θp, the whisker bends in the other direction and sobj increases.
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical modeling results.

claim: When the object is close to the face (small d), the whisker contacts the object near its base and a static solution exists for most practical θp values.
source: When the object is close to the face (small d), the whisker contacts the object near its base and a static solution exists for most practical θp values (peak-to-peak amplitude of whisker movements, 50° [Voigts et al., 2008; Curtis and Kleinfeld, 2009; O'Connor et al., 2013]).
evidence: The claim is supported by theoretical modeling and citations to prior research on whisker movement amplitudes.

claim: For larger d, the θp regime with a stable solution decreases approximately linearly for conical whiskers.
source: For larger d, the θp regime with a stable solution decreases approximately linearly.
evidence: The claim is supported by theoretical modeling shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The range of θp with a stable solution is larger for the CF than the CB configuration.
source: The range of θp with a stable solution is larger for the CF than the CB configuration.
evidence: The claim is supported by theoretical modeling shown in Figure 3E.

claim: In the CB configuration the intrinsic curvature aids slip-off.
source: This is consistent with experimental observations (Quist and Hartmann, 2012) and intuition: in the CB configuration the intrinsic curvature aids slip-off.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research and physical intuition.

claim: When the object touches near the whisker tip (large d), the saddle-node bifurcation ceases to exist and the whisker is 'pulled off' the object.
source: When the object touches near the whisker tip (large d), the saddle-node bifurcation ceases to exist and the whisker is 'pulled off' the object. (Figure 3E, blue line).
evidence: The claim is supported by theoretical modeling shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The pull-offs are the result of whisker truncation, and would not occur for a perfect cone.
source: The pull-offs are the result of whisker truncation, and would not occur for a perfect cone.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the theoretical model.

claim: Cylindrical whiskers exhibit stable solutions at much larger θp compared to conical whiskers.
source: Although the bifurcation diagrams were superficially similar for conical and cylindrical whiskers (c.f. Figure 3B–E,G–J), cylindrical whiskers exhibit stable solutions at much larger θp.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of theoretical modeling results in Figures 3B-E and 3G-J.

claim: For cylindrical whiskers, the SNB occurs for θp > 90°, which is beyond plausible ranges of whisking since whiskers cannot move into the face.
source: The SNB occurs for θp > 90° (Figure 3G–I, black lines and solid circles; d = 10 mm), which is beyond plausible ranges of whisking since whiskers cannot move into the face.
evidence: The claim is supported by theoretical modeling shown in Figure 3G-I and physical constraints.

claim: When cylindrical whiskers touch the object close to their end, they are pulled off at moderate θp, because the whisker tip reaches the object.
source: When cylindrical whiskers touch the object close to their end, they are pulled off at moderate θp, because the whisker tip reaches the object (Figure 3I, blue line) sobj = LW.
evidence: The claim is supported by theoretical modeling shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Cylindrical whiskers do not slip-off the pole.
source: Therefore, cylindrical whiskers do not slip-off the pole.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the theoretical modeling results.

claim: For a homogenous cylinder, the lack of slip-off is independent of the cylinder's bending stiffness and thus its thickness.
source: For a homogenous cylinder this effect is independent of the cylinder's bending stiffness and thus its thickness.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the theoretical model.

claim: The model predicts that conical and cylindrical whiskers interact with objects in a fundamentally different way.
source: Our model thus predicts that conical and cylindrical whiskers interact with objects in a fundamentally different way.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the theoretical modeling results.

claim: For a large range of object distances conical whiskers slip past objects, whereas cylindrical whiskers get stuck.
source: For a large range of object distances conical whiskers slip past objects, whereas cylindrical whiskers get stuck.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the theoretical modeling results.

claim: Mouse and human hair have similar Young's Modulus.
source: Mouse and human hair have similar Young's Modulus (Hu et al., 2010; Quist et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: As the mouse whisker rotated into the pole it was deformed until, at a critical θp, it suddenly slipped off the pole.
source: As the whisker rotated into the pole it was deformed until, at a critical θp, it suddenly slipped off the pole (Figure 4B, Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Video 1.

claim: Whisker slip-offs occurred before the tip of the whisker had reached the point of contact.
source: Whisker slip-offs occurred before the tip of the whisker had reached the point of contact.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations in Figure 4B.

claim: For the cylindrical hair, slip-offs did not occur.
source: In contrast, for the cylindrical hair, slip-offs did not occur.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations in Figure 4C.

claim: For cylindrical hair, detachments always coincided with the whisker tip reaching the point of contact and were thus pull-offs.
source: Detachments always coincided with the whisker tip reaching the point of contact and were thus pull-offs (Figure 4C, red line, Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Video 2.

claim: The experimental results for whisker-object interactions were in agreement with the model.
source: The experimental results were in agreement with the model.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of experimental data and theoretical predictions in Figure 4D.

claim: For conical whiskers, slip-off occurred before the whisker tip reached the object, and the critical θp decreased rapidly with object distance.
source: For conical whiskers, slip-off occurred before the whisker tip reached the object, and the critical θp decreased rapidly with object distance (Figure 4D, black circles).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The observed deviations between the idealized conical model and actual whisker are expected because the whisker is not a perfect cone and because the whisker's Young's modulus may vary slightly along its length.
source: The observed deviations between the idealized conical model and actual whisker are expected because the whisker is not a perfect cone (Ibrahim and Wright, 1975) and because the whisker's Young's modulus may vary slightly along its length (Quist et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from known whisker properties and citations to prior research.

claim: The cylindrical hair only pulled off when the whisker tip reached the pole, with a close fit between experimental and theoretical results.
source: In contrast, the cylindrical hair only pulled off when the whisker tip reached the pole (Figure 4C), with a close fit between experimental and theoretical results (Figure 4D, blue circles).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of experimental data and theoretical predictions in Figure 4D.

claim: Slip-offs occur normally during whisker-dependent behavior.
source: We next tested if slip-offs occur normally during whisker-dependent behavior (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behaving mice shown in Figure 5.

claim: Slip-offs were more likely for more distant object locations in behaving mice.
source: Slip-offs were more likely for more distant object locations (Figure 5B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Slip-offs occurred at larger θp for smaller object distances in behaving mice.
source: and occurred at larger θp for smaller object distances (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Slip-offs occurred in approximately 15% of behavioral trials.
source: Overall, slip-offs occurred in approximately 15% of behavioral trials.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behaving mice.

claim: For objects touching the whisker near the tip, detachments occurred for small θp (<20°), with the whisker tip reaching the pole (i.e., pull-offs).
source: For objects touching the whisker near the tip, detachments occurred for small θp (<20°), with the whisker tip reaching the pole (i.e., pull-offs).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: For smaller object distances slip-off occurred at larger θp (>20°), consistent with a saddle-node bifurcation (i.e., slip-offs).
source: For smaller object distances slip-off occurred at larger θp (>20°), consistent with a saddle-node bifurcation (i.e., slip-offs).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and comparison with theoretical predictions.

claim: The critical θp values for slip-off varied significantly across trials even for identical object distances.
source: The critical θp values for slip-off varied significantly across trials even for identical object distances.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations in Figure 5C.

claim: The variability in critical θp values is likely caused by differences in whisker movement and whisker elevation across trials.
source: This variability is likely caused by differences in whisker movement and whisker elevation across trials.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on reasoning about potential sources of variability.

claim: Mice can discriminate surface roughness over a few whisking cycles.
source: For example, mice can discriminate surface roughness over a few whisking cycles (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2013.

claim: Texture is likely inferred from the statistics of whisker micromotions produced by the interactions between whiskers and objects.
source: Texture is likely inferred from the statistics of whisker micromotions produced by the interactions between whiskers and objects (Diamond, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Diamond, 2010.

claim: As whiskers move over objects whiskers occasionally get stuck, followed by high-velocity slips.
source: In particular, as whiskers move over objects whiskers occasionally get stuck, followed by high-velocity slips.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about whisker-texture interactions.

claim: The pattern of stick-slip events is highly informative about surface texture.
source: The pattern of stick-slip events is highly informative about surface texture (Arabzadeh et al., 2005; Wolfe et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The tips of mouse whiskers moved along the surface in an irregular manner, during protractions and retractions.
source: The tips of mouse whiskers moved along the surface in an irregular manner, during protractions and retractions.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations in Figure 6B.

claim: Whisker tips were transiently trapped followed by small, high-velocity slips.
source: Whisker tips were transiently trapped (Figure 6B, red) followed by small, high-velocity slips (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: The pattern of stick-slip events differed for different wall distances.
source: The pattern of stick-slip events differed for different wall distances (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: As cylindrical hairs swept across the surface they were trapped during initial protraction and remained trapped for the remainder of the experiment lasting multiple whisking cycles.
source: In contrast, as cylindrical hairs swept across the surface they were trapped during initial protraction and remained trapped for the remainder of the experiment lasting multiple whisking cycles (Figure 6D–F, Video 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D-F and Video 4.

claim: When the distance between follicle and the site of trapping was shorter than the hair length, the hair buckled out of the plane of movement.
source: When the distance between follicle and the site of trapping was shorter than the hair length, the hair buckled out of the plane of movement (Figure 6E, top).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations in Figure 6E.

claim: The tips of hairs escaped the traps only when the distance to the tip along the path of an undeflected hair exceeded the actual hair arclength.
source: The tips of hairs escaped the traps only when the distance to the tip along the path of an undeflected hair exceeded the actual hair arclength (Figure 6E,F, pane 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations in Figure 6E and 6F.

claim: The conical whisker shape is critical for the sweeping motions of whisker tips across objects and surfaces, which supports feature extraction via stick-slip events.
source: These measurements show that the conical whisker shape is critical for the sweeping motions of whisker tips across objects and surfaces, which supports feature extraction via stick-slip events.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results in Figure 6.

claim: Conical whiskers can move past walls and objects, which may be critical for positioning of whiskers in confined spaces, such as tunnels, during directed tactile exploration.
source: More generally, conical whiskers can move past walls and objects, which may be critical for positioning of whiskers in confined spaces, such as tunnels, during directed tactile exploration.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: The first touch within a trial caused a large peak in activity with a rapid rise in barrel cortex.
source: The first touch within a trial caused a large peak in activity with a rapid rise (Figure 7B,C), consistent with previous work (Simons, 1978; Armstrong-James et al., 1992; de Kock et al., 2007; O'Connor et al., 2010b; O'Connor et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and 7C and citations to prior research.

claim: Later touches within a series, during which slip-offs were more commonly seen, produced smaller responses in barrel cortex.
source: Later touches within a series, during which slip-offs were more commonly seen, produced smaller responses (Figure 7D) (Ahissar et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D and a citation to Ahissar et al., 2001.

claim: When slip-off did not occur, the detach-related signals were almost undetectable.
source: When slip-off did not occur, the detach-related signals were almost undetectable.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: When slip-off did occur, the detach-related signals were large, comparable to the first touch.
source: In contrast, when slip-off did occur, the detach-related signals were large, comparable to the first touch (Figure 7F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F and 7G.

claim: Tapered whiskers have resonance frequencies that are robust to wear and truncation damage to their tips.
source: Tapered whiskers have resonance frequencies that are robust to wear and truncation damage to their tips (Williams and Kramer, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Williams and Kramer, 2010.

claim: Tapered whiskers detach from objects at shallower push angles than cylindrical whisker substitutes.
source: Tapered whiskers also detach from objects at shallower push angles than cylindrical whisker substitutes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Tapered whiskers slip-off when the contact point is along the whisker body (sobj < Lw), whereas cylindrical hairs require the tip to be pulled off (sobj = Lw) for biologically plausible push angles.
source: Here we go beyond prior observations and uncover fundamental differences in how tapered and untapered hairs interact with objects; tapered whiskers slip-off when the contact point is along the whisker body (sobj < Lw), whereas cylindrical hairs require the tip to be pulled off (sobj = Lw) for biologically plausible push angles (Figure 3E,J, Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by theoretical modeling and experimental data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Tapered whiskers have greater freedom of movement past obstacles compared to cylindrical hairs.
source: Thus, tapered whiskers have greater freedom of movement past obstacles compared to cylindrical hairs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental and theoretical results.

claim: This mobility is seen in reduced preparations and also during active behavior, as whisker slip-off occurs in a variety of object location discrimination tasks.
source: This mobility is seen in reduced preparations (Figure 4) and also during active behavior, as whisker slip-off occurs in a variety of object location discrimination tasks (Figures 5, 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 4, 5, and 7.

claim: The intrinsic difference in detachment produces qualitatively different interaction patterns during palpation of textured surfaces.
source: The intrinsic difference in detachment also produces qualitatively different interaction patterns during palpation of textured surfaces (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: Tapered whiskers sweep past with stick-slip micromotions, whereas cylindrical whiskers become immobilized on surface imperfections.
source: Tapered whiskers sweep past with stick-slip micromotions, whereas cylindrical whiskers become immobilized on surface imperfections.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: For conical whiskers there are only two possible solutions for whisker shape for a given object distance and push angle, one stable, one unstable.
source: We demonstrate that for conical whiskers there are only two possible solutions for whisker shape for a given object distance and push angle, one stable, one unstable.
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical modeling results.

claim: Slip-offs occur suddenly at a critical push angle, θp, corresponding to the angle where saddle-node bifurcations occur.
source: Slip-offs occur suddenly at a critical push angle, θp, corresponding to the angle where these saddle-node bifurcations occur.
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical modeling and interpretation.

claim: For conical whiskers the critical push angles are within the normal range of whisking.
source: For conical whiskers the critical push angles are within the normal range of whisking (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: For cylindrical hairs the critical angles fall outside the range of whisking.
source: For cylindrical hairs the critical angles fall outside the range of whisking.
evidence: The claim is supported by theoretical modeling in Figure 3.

claim: Truncations of conical whiskers make whisker behavior more 'cylindrical-like'.
source: Truncations of conical whiskers make whisker behavior more 'cylindrical-like' (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: In situations where the whisker curvature was contained within a plane, the agreement between theory and experiment was very good.
source: In situations where the whisker curvature was contained within a plane, the agreement between theory and experiment was very good (Figure 4), despite our model ignoring frictional forces.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of theoretical predictions and experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: The small remnant differences between theory and experiment are due to deviations of whisker geometry from perfect conical shape and possible inhomogeneities in the Young's modulus.
source: The small remnant differences between theory and experiment are due to deviations of whisker geometry from perfect conical shape (AH, KS, DG, unpublished) and possible inhomogeneities in the Young's modulus (Quist et al., 2011) (but also see Carl et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from known whisker properties and citations to prior research.

claim: In behaving mice the whisker droops out of the plane of whisking.
source: In behaving mice the whisker droops out of the plane of whisking (Towal et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Towal et al., 2011.

claim: Rigorous treatment of whisker deflection by an object would require a three-dimensional model.
source: Rigorous treatment of whisker deflection by an object would thus require a three-dimensional model.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the three-dimensional nature of whisker movements.

claim: Many rodents, including house mice and African pouched mice, live in group nests consisting of chambers connected by long, body-width tunnels.
source: Within their natural habitat, many rodents, including house mice (Berry, 1968) and African pouched mice (Ellison, 1993), live in group nests consisting of chambers connected by long, body-width tunnels.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research on rodent ecology.

claim: During running, whiskers point forward to touch unanticipated objects.
source: During running, whiskers point forward to touch unanticipated objects.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about rodent whisker behavior.

claim: When a new object is encountered rodents foveate their whiskers on the object for fine-scale exploration.
source: When a new object is encountered rodents foveate their whiskers on the object for fine-scale exploration (Grant et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Grant et al., 2009.

claim: Within dark, radially constrained tunnels, navigation, localization of objects, social touch, and determination of friend or foe demands freedom of whisker motion.
source: Within these dark, radially constrained tunnels, navigation (Vincent, 1912; Dehnhardt et al., 2001), localization of objects (Hutson and Masterton, 1986; Krupa et al., 2001), social touch (Wolfe et al., 2011), and determination of friend or foe (Anjum et al., 2006) demands freedom of whisker motion.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from cited research on whisker functions and the constraints of tunnel environments.

claim: Whiskers have to be moved past the rough walls of the tunnel.
source: Whiskers have to be moved past the rough walls of the tunnel.
evidence: The claim is based on inference about the requirements for whisker function in tunnels.

claim: Without the flexibility provided by whisker taper, the whiskers could be trapped in a far protracted or retracted orientation, causing a tactile 'blind-spot'.
source: Without the flexibility provided by whisker taper, the whiskers could be trapped in a far protracted or retracted orientation, causing a tactile 'blind-spot'.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: A major sensory avenue for the localization and identification of objects and their properties is via directed sweeping of whiskers across object surfaces.
source: A major sensory avenue for the localization and identification of objects and their properties is via directed sweeping of whiskers across object surfaces (Carvell and Simons, 1990; Ritt et al., 2008; von Heimendahl et al., 2007; Wolfe et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: During artificial periodic palpation of fine-grained textures, conical whiskers traversed the surface with complex micromotions, whereas cylindrical hair became trapped against the surface.
source: During artificial periodic palpation of fine-grained textures, conical whiskers traversed the surface with complex micromotions, whereas cylindrical hair became trapped against the surface (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: It is likely that forces at the tip build up until they bend the whisker tip sufficiently to free it from traps.
source: Although a precise understanding of the interaction between a tapered whisker and textured surface during a stick-slip event has not been treated mathematically, it is likely that forces at the tip build up until they bend the whisker tip sufficiently to free it from traps.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on physical reasoning.

claim: In the cylindrical case, the constant bending stiffness of the body and tip render the whisker incapable of transmitting sufficient lateral force to buckle the much stiffer tip and release it from the surface.
source: In the cylindrical case, the constant bending stiffness of the body and tip render the whisker incapable of transmitting sufficient lateral force to buckle the much stiffer tip and release it from the surface.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the mechanical properties of cylindrical structures.

claim: During active whisking, stick-slip micromotions on textured surfaces drive sparse, precisely timed spikes in barrel cortex that provide a sensory cue for surface texture.
source: During active whisking, stick-slip micromotions on textured surfaces drive sparse, precisely timed spikes in barrel cortex that provide a sensory cue for surface texture (Jadhav et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jadhav et al., 2009.

claim: Neural responses in barrel cortex to repeated contacts between whiskers and objects show strong adaptation during active touch and object location discrimination.
source: Neural responses in barrel cortex to repeated contacts between whiskers and objects show strong adaptation during active touch (Ahissar et al., 2001; Crochet et al., 2011) and object location discrimination (Figure 7C,D,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research and experimental data in Figure 7.

claim: Despite occurring when the circuit is adapted to touch, slip-offs produce strong volleys of cortical activity, of comparable magnitude to pre-adapted touch.
source: Despite occurring when the circuit is adapted to touch, slip-offs produce strong volleys of cortical activity, of comparable magnitude to pre-adapted touch (Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 7F.

claim: Slip-related excitation can overcome cortical touch adaptation and likely contributes to sensation and perception in a variety of tactile behaviors.
source: Thus, slip-related excitation can overcome cortical touch adaptation and likely contributes to sensation and perception in a variety of tactile behaviors (Arabzadeh et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the experimental results and a citation to prior research.

claim: Whiskers were modeled as truncated cones with a cylindrical cross section, base radius rbase, tip radius rtip, and length LW.
source: We modeled rodent whiskers as truncated cones with a cylindrical cross section, base radius rbase, tip radius rtip, and length LW (Ibrahim and Wright, 1975; Boubenec et al., 2012) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim describes the theoretical model used in the study, with citations to prior work.

claim: Whiskers have intrinsic curvature and are further deflected by forces that are caused by interactions with objects.
source: Whiskers have intrinsic curvature (Quist and Hartmann, 2012) and are further deflected by forces that are caused by interactions with objects (O'Connor et al., 2010a; Bagdasarian et al., 2013; Pammer et al., 2013) (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Contacts occurred either in the 'concave backward' (CB) or 'concave forward' (CF) directions.
source: In our model, contacts occurred either in the 'concave backward' (CB) or 'concave forward' (CF) directions (Figure 1C) (Quist and Hartmann, 2012).
evidence: The claim describes the model setup, with a citation to prior work.

claim: Contact strength was quantified using the push angle θp, the angle through which the whisker is rotated into the object.
source: We quantified contact strength using the push angle θp (Quist and Hartmann, 2012), the angle through which the whisker is rotated into the object (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim describes the model parameter, with a citation to prior work.

claim: Whisker shape was computed by solving the Euler–Bernoulli beam equation in the quasi-static regime.
source: We computed whisker shape by solving the Euler–Bernoulli beam equation in the quasi-static regime (Euler, 1744; Birdwell et al., 2007; Solomon and Hartmann, 2006; Pammer et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim describes the theoretical method, with citations to prior work.

claim: The object was assumed to be a cylindrical pole perpendicular to the plane of motion.
source: The object was assumed to be a cylindrical pole perpendicular to the plane of motion, as is typically used in object localization experiments (Knutsen et al., 2006; Mehta et al., 2007; O'Connor et al., 2010a; Pammer et al., 2013) (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim describes the model setup, with citations to prior experimental work.

claim: The whisker shape at each time was determined by the static solution computed for the time-varying boundary conditions.
source: The whisker shape at each time was determined by the static solution computed for the time-varying boundary conditions.
evidence: The claim describes the theoretical approach used in the model.
